title: Knitting
wiki_lead:
Knitting is the process of interlooping a continuous length of yarn to create textile fabric made of rows of interconnected loops. Knitting can be done by hand, by machine or using one of a variety of frames developed for the purpose. When done by hand, one uses a pair of knitting needles where the loops are created one at a time. When done by machine the loops are created on hooks that work one entire row of knitting at a time.
Hand knitting needles are either straight with blunt ends or so-called "circular needles" that are a single flexible tube or wire with blunt needles at both ends. The resulting knitted fabric consists rows of loops that intermesh with the rows above and below.
Differences in yarn (varying in fiber type, yarn weight, color, uniformity, twist per inch), in needle size, and in stitch type allow for a variety of knitted fabrics with different properties, including texture, thickness, heat retention, and water resistance. A small sample of knitwork is known as a "swatch" and helps the maker determine the gauge of the intended work.

Overview


Etymology of the words knit and knitting
There are several possible origins of the word knit and knitting. These include the German derivation from the word knutten (to tie), the Old Norse word knytja, and the Old English words cnyttan (to tie a knot, bind together, fasten by tieing) and cnotta (knot).


History and culture

Artifacts of fabric making using some form of knitting have been found in many regions including Egypt, China, Denmark, and Sweden, dating as far back as 4200 BCE. The exact origins of the invention of knitting are unknown, however the earliest known examples are cotton socks dating from the 11th century, found in the remains of the city of Fustat, now part of Cairo. In Europe, knitting is believed to be an evolution of the ancient craft of nålebinding, the Scandinavian word for "needle binding". In nålebinding, fabric is created through forming loops and knots of yarn with a single needle.
The first commercial knitting guilds appeared in Western Europe in the early fifteenth century (Tournai in 1429, Barcelona in 1496). The Guild of Saint Fiacre was founded in Paris in 1527, but the archives mention an organization (not necessarily a guild) of knitters from 1268. The occupation "cap knitter" was recorded in 1473 as these textile artists primarily produced knit caps and dyed stockings.
In 1589, William Lee of Nottinghamshire invented the first stocking frame, which was an early form of the knitting machine. Lee petitioned Queen Elizabeth I for a patent but was denied due to the coarse nature of the frame-knit fabric and the fear that frame knitting would take away the jobs of hand knitters in England. Lee improved the knitting frame to accommodate a finer gauge, or number of stitches per inch, producing a smoother fabric, but his petition for a patent failed following the death of his court sponsor and apprentice, Lord Hunsdon, in 1596. Lee travelled to Normandy, France, and later Paris, along with a group of apprentices in search of court sponsorship for his invention. After further trials and tribulations due to the assassination of King Henry IV in 1610, Lee was unable to establish a successful business in Paris. William Lee died in Paris in 1614, and his brother James Lee along with William's apprentice, Aston, adopted the petition to patent the knitting machine in England. By 1620, frame knitting was an established mode of production of knitted garments.
With the invention of the stocking frame, knitting "by hand" became a craft used by country people with easy access to fiber. Similar to quilting, spinning, and needlepoint, hand knitting became a leisure activity for the wealthy.

This process produces stretchable, durable materials prized for their elasticity and warmth, distinguishing it from weaving, which interlaces yarns at right angles. The origins of knitting trace back to ancient Egypt, where the oldest surviving examplesâred and white cotton socks using a single-needle technique known as nÃ¥lbindning, a precursor to modern knittingâdate to the 3rd to 5th centuries AD. True two-needle knitting emerged later in the Middle East and spread to Europe via Muslim artisans in Spain by the 12th century, with early European items including ceremonial gloves and cushion covers. The craft gained prominence in Europe during the Renaissance, fueled by demand for knitted stockings, and underwent mechanization in 1589 when English clergyman William Lee invented the first knitting frame, a hand-powered machine that revolutionized hosiery production. Knitting encompasses hand and machine methods, with hand knitting involving basic stitches such as the knit (forming a V-shaped loop) and purl (creating a horizontal ridge) to build flat or circular fabrics, often using two or more straight or circular needles. Materials range from natural fibers like wool, cotton, and silk âsourced historically from sheep, plants, and silkwormsâto modern synthetics such as acrylic and nylon, enabling diverse applications from garments and accessories to medical textiles and technical fabrics. Today, knitting supports both artisanal traditions and industrial manufacturing, with the global knitwear market valued at approximately USD 908 billion as of 2024.
